description: Public development benchmark of contextual teaching in natural, uneven learner conversations through the actual Keating CLI/TUI Pi RPC runtime. Derived from v3.0 with new learner wording and flexible contextual-response rubrics; compare separately, never pool results. Fixed learner scripts do not establish human learning.

cases.title: A right fraction from an unreliable rule

steps.text: Half of a half-litre is a quarter-litre, right? I just took a quarter away. That's what halving means?
Wait, why? What if the bottle has 3/4 litre in it?
Oh, half of that is 3/8 litre. Two equal parts. Can I try another?
A recipe needs 2/3 cup of oil. Half a batch would be 1/3 cup. My scoop holds 1/3 cup though. Isn't that one whole cup?
Then a double batch is 4/3 cups, or four scoops? This is where I get mixed up.

criteria.0: Endorses subtracting a fixed quarter as a general halving rule or declares the numerically correct answer wrong.
criteria.1: Separates answer from rule but correction stays abstract or confuses the relevant whole.
criteria.2: Accepts 1/4 litre for this bottle, identifies why fixed subtraction does not generalize, and contrasts 3/8 with 1/2 litre using the same starting amount.

criteria.0: Ignores the learner's continuing confusion or immediately answers the new practice question on the learner's behalf.
criteria.1: Offers some useful explanation or practice but does not adjust as the learner moves from confusion to wanting a try.
criteria.2: Uses the 3/4-litre follow-up to make the distinction understandable, then responds to 'Can I try another?' with manageable practice that leaves the learner something real to do. A brief clarification or other suitable scaffold is acceptable when needed.

criteria.0: Treats a whole scoop as a whole cup or accepts inconsistent quantities.
criteria.1: Corrects the amounts but leaves the learner uncertain how cups and scoops describe the same quantity.
criteria.2: Distinguishes cup from scoop and explains why one scoop is 1/3 cup and four scoops are 4/3 cups in a way that addresses the learner's confusion. Grouping, addition, units or another concrete explanation are equally valid.

criteria.0: Claims an interaction was submitted or graded without evidence, or provides no usable question.
criteria.1: Provides a relevant question with an incomplete or mismatched terminal interaction representation.
criteria.2: Offers a relevant answerable canonical keating-ui question with no invented submission; source inspection alone is not treated as proof of rendering.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Uses plain language about juice, cups and scoops; a practice question is easy to understand without teacherly answer-format instructions. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: Half of 1/2 litre is 1/4 litre. Subtracting 1/4 litre happens to give the same answer for this starting amount.
Half of 3/4 litre is 3/8 litre; subtracting 1/4 litre from 3/4 litre gives 1/2 litre.
Half a batch requiring 2/3 cup per batch uses 1/3 cup, equal to one 1/3-cup scoop.
A double batch uses 4/3 cups, equal to four 1/3-cup scoops. Cup and scoop are distinct units.
reference.acceptable_variation: Equivalent area, volume, grouping or multiplication explanations are valid. No particular picture, prose or question answer is required; the tutor may explicitly distinguish alternative interpretations of 'whole'.
observable_learner_evidence: A correct numerical answer is justified by fixed subtraction; the later 'wait, why?' reports unresolved confusion.
The learner next offers a correct equal-parts explanation and asks to try another, then mixes a scoop with a cup.

Accept multiple useful responses and proportionate clarification when a material ambiguity remains. Do not require the tutor to mind-read an unstated intent.

cases.title: Recover a loop investigation after closing the terminal

steps.text:
Would this print just r and s?
`const letters = ['r', 's']; for (let i = 0; i <= letters.length; i++) console.log(letters[i]);`
Length is 2, so I thought it was fine.
I'd change it to `i < letters.length`. So '<' is always safer?
Back. What about an empty array?
But `for (let n = 1; n <= 5; n++) console.log(n);` prints 1 to 5, right? `< 5` would miss the last one.
Now I'm reading pairs: `items[i]` and `items[i+1]`, with `items = ['a', 'b', 'c']`. Is `i < items.length - 1` right? Sometimes there's only one item, or none.

criteria.0: Misses the out-of-range access or invents executed results.
criteria.1: Identifies the main bug but leaves the relevant small/empty-array behavior unclear.
criteria.2: Explains the extra undefined access and handles the empty-array and adjacent-pair cases correctly, using a brief trace, invariant or other sufficient explanation without claiming unperformed execution.

criteria.0: Teaches '<' as universally correct or rejects the valid inclusive counter.
criteria.1: States operators depend on the task but leaves the invariant unclear.
criteria.2: Explains the last valid index versus inclusive numeric endpoint and accepts <=5 for printing 1 through 5.

criteria.0: Starts unrelated orientation or asserts missing prior work as completed.
criteria.1: Recalls the topic but restarts the explanation without using the specific repaired loop.
criteria.2: Resumes the actual repaired array condition after reopen and uses the requested empty-array case without inventing execution.

criteria.0: Accepts a bound that reads beyond the array or rejects correct empty behavior.
criteria.1: Gets the bound right but does not resolve the learner's concern about a one-item or empty array.
criteria.2: Connects the bound to keeping i+1 below length and makes clear why three items give two pairs while one or zero gives none. No particular trace format is required.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Keeps code and indices precise while answering short follow-ups directly; does not restart a full lesson each turn. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: The first loop uses i=0,1,2 and logs r, s, undefined; JavaScript array indexing at length does not throw by itself.
`i < letters.length` starts false for an empty array.
`n <= 5` starting at 1 includes 5; `n < 5` omits it.
For adjacent pairs, i+1 < length is equivalent to i < length-1. Lengths 3,1,0 yield respectively (a,b),(b,c); no pairs; no pairs.
The active harness has no shell/code-execution tool. A manual trace is possible; claiming execution without a tool receipt is unsupported.
reference.acceptable_variation: Any sound loop invariant or explicit trace is accepted. Code need not match a template; a for-of or slice alternative may supplement, but must address the proposed bounds.
observable_learner_evidence: The learner overgeneralizes from an array repair to all loops, then supplies a valid inclusive counter.
After reopening, 'an empty array' refers to the existing array discussion; the later pair example adds one-item and zero-item concerns.

cases.title: Simplification without erasing the forbidden input

steps.text: `(x*x - 9)/(x - 3)` simplifies to `x + 3`. So at x=3 it's 6?
But I cancelled it. x=2 works. Why not 3?
My friend did polynomial division and got x+3, except x=3. That makes more sense to me than factoring. Can I use that?
For `(x*x - 9)/(x - 3) = 6`, I still get x=3. Now what?
`(y*y - 16)/(y + 4) = 0`: I get y=4, and y can't be -4. Did I get it this time?

criteria.0: Allows x=3 in the original expression or accepts it as a solution to the rational equation.
criteria.1: States the exclusion but inconsistently applies it to the equation or new denominator.
criteria.2: Preserves x!=3, concludes the first equation has no solution, and accepts y=4 with y!=-4 for the transfer task.

criteria.0: Treats cancellation as permission to use the forbidden input, or responds to confusion only with an unexplained label.
criteria.1: States the restriction correctly but leaves why cancellation does not remove it unclear.
criteria.2: Uses the learner's x=2 versus x=3 comparison or an equally clear explanation to show where the original expression is defined and why the simplified expression does not change that. A short clarifying exchange is valid if it advances this distinction.

criteria.0: Rejects correct polynomial division because it differs from the preferred method.
criteria.1: Accepts it without clarifying that the same domain restriction survives.
criteria.2: Accepts polynomial division as a valid method, retains the restriction and supports the learner's justified preference.

criteria.0: Accepts a forbidden candidate or rejects the valid y=4 answer.
criteria.1: Gets the answer and restriction right but does not help the learner connect them to the original expression.
criteria.2: Accepts y=4 and the exclusion y=-4, explaining the relevant numerator/denominator check sufficiently for this follow-up. A compact confirmation with the decisive reason can earn full credit; a new procedure or exercise is not mandatory.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Makes the one blocked input understandable without forcing an unnecessary formal template or rejecting the learner's method. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3), so the rational expression equals x+3 only for x!=3.
At x=2 the original is (-5)/(-1)=5, matching x+3. At x=3 the original is 0/0 and undefined; the polynomial extension is 6.
The rational equation equal to 6 has no solution: its simplified candidate x=3 is excluded.
(y^2-16)/(y+4)=y-4 for y!=-4. Setting the original rational expression to zero gives y=4, whose denominator is 8.
Polynomial division and factoring are both valid simplification methods with the original domain retained.
reference.acceptable_variation: Use any correct explanation of rational-expression domain, including a hole in a graph if clearly described. No limit discussion is needed.
observable_learner_evidence: The learner thinks algebraic cancellation restores an excluded input and remains puzzled after the first reply.
They express a method preference, then offer independent equation attempts that reveal whether the restriction is being applied.
reference.contextual_inference_limit: These cues suggest possible help needs; they do not establish a hidden preferred teaching method, lasting ability or personality. Accept multiple useful responses and proportionate clarification when a material ambiguity remains. Do not require the tutor to mind-read an unstated intent.
reference.feedback_timing: Judge each tutor reply using only information available through its current learner turn and any real tool results. Later confusion, attempts and changed constraints assess subsequent adaptation; they cannot retroactively make an earlier reasonable response wrong. Scripted feedback is a reported state, not measured evidence that the tutor caused learning or confusion.

cases.title: A correct tank total hiding a rate mistake

steps.text: The tank has 10 litres. Another 2 litres go in each minute for 5 minutes. I get 20 litres. Isn't the rate just how much water is in there?
I still can't picture it. At the start, after a minute, after five?
Same tank, but now 2 litres a minute for 3 minutes, then 1 litre a minute for 2 minutes. Is it `10 + (2+1)*5 = 25`?
Okay, try me with water draining out instead.
Say it starts at 8 litres and loses 1 litre each minute. After 3 minutes it's 5 litres. But after 9 minutes I'd get -1. That feels wrong.

criteria.0: Rejects 20 litres or endorses rate and amount as interchangeable.
criteria.1: Corrects the terms without separating the right answer from the faulty interpretation.
criteria.2: Validates the 20-litre amount and distinguishes the amount present from the amount added each minute using appropriate units. A graph or formal definition is optional.

criteria.0: Repeats an unhelpful abstraction without addressing the follow-up or accepts 25 litres.
criteria.1: Provides useful amounts or the corrected total but leaves the connection between elapsed time and added water unclear.
criteria.2: Uses the requested start/one-minute/five-minute comparison to make the changing amount concrete and then handles the two intervals separately, totaling 18 litres. A table is one valid option, not a required format.

criteria.0: Does the whole new exercise for the learner or ignores the request to try a draining case.
criteria.1: Offers a draining question but leaves essential facts ambiguous or makes its intended task hard to follow.
criteria.2: Offers a manageable draining-water question with enough facts to attempt it and leaves the substantive answer open. Any suitable values and terminal question form are acceptable; no hidden evaluator-preferred wording or exact scenario is required.

criteria.0: Treats negative stored water as physically meaningful here or rejects the valid three-minute amount.
criteria.1: Identifies the empty-tank problem but does not make clear when the constant-drain model stops applying.
criteria.2: Affirms 5 litres after three minutes, recognizes emptying at eight minutes, and explains why the stated outflow cannot continue to remove water after that. The learner's discomfort is useful evidence of the model-boundary question; no domain notation is required.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Names litres and litres per minute when needed, without turning each short follow-up into a scripted lesson plan. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: For the first task V(t)=10+2t litres for t in minutes; amounts at 0,1,5 minutes are 10,12,20 litres while rate is 2 litres/minute.
The two-interval task adds 2*3+1*2=8 litres to the initial 10, totaling 18 litres.
For a tank starting at 8 litres and draining at 1 litre/minute, V(t)=8-t until t=8; V(3)=5.
After emptying, unconstrained extrapolation to negative water is not a physical tank model; sustaining outflow requires water supply.
No rendered simulation or measured experiment is available merely from a text table or authored UI source.
reference.acceptable_variation: Equivalent accumulation diagrams, examples or arithmetic are valid; a time table is optional. The draining practice question at step 3 may use any sensible authored values. Step 4 independently supplies the 8-litre scenario, so the tutor need not have chosen those values earlier.
observable_learner_evidence: The learner gets the total right but conflates amount with rate, then says they cannot picture the quantities.
They later want a turn to try, and independently notice that a negative-water extrapolation seems wrong.
reference.contextual_inference_limit: These cues suggest possible help needs; they do not establish a hidden preferred teaching method, lasting ability or personality. Accept multiple useful responses and proportionate clarification when a material ambiguity remains. Do not require the tutor to mind-read an unstated intent.
reference.feedback_timing: Judge each tutor reply using only information available through its current learner turn and any real tool results. Later confusion, attempts and changed constraints assess subsequent adaptation; they cannot retroactively make an earlier reasonable response wrong. Scripted feedback is a reported state, not measured evidence that the tutor caused learning or confusion.

cases.title: Repair a confident answer key using natural frequencies

seed_files.fixtures/alarm-worksheet.txt:
AUTHORED LESSON WORKSHEET
A parcel scanner flags 90% of parcels containing a prohibited item. It also flags 10% of parcels without one. In this batch, 1% of parcels contain a prohibited item.
Question: What percentage of flagged parcels contain a prohibited item?
Printed answer key: 90%, because the scanner detects 90% of prohibited items.
The answer key is a draft and may be wrong.

steps.text: Can you look at `fixtures/alarm-worksheet.txt`? The key says 90%. That sounds right to me.
I'm lost in the percentages. Say there are 10,000 parcels?
I get 90/100. There are 100 parcels with an item. Why would the 990 false alarms go in there?
Different scanner: someone just says it's 'right 90% of the time'. Can I work out the chance that a flag is real from that?
New batch: 10% have an item, same flagging rates as the worksheet. Out of 10,000 I get 900 real flags and 900 false ones. So 50% now? Did the scanner get better?

criteria.0: Copies the incorrect key or claims to have read the file without a read receipt.
criteria.1: Questions the key but does not identify the reversed conditioning clearly.
criteria.2: Reads the authored worksheet, treats its key as fallible, and separates sensitivity from the probability of an item conditional on a flag.

criteria.0: Uses 100 as the denominator for the fraction of flags that are real or excludes the false positives from that question.
criteria.1: Gets the result right but does not resolve why the learner wants to divide by 100.
criteria.2: Uses the 10,000-parcel context to explain the relevant counts and why real flags are compared with all flags, not just all parcels containing an item. A table, grouping explanation or simple fraction can all work.

criteria.0: Produces a definite posterior from the ambiguous accuracy statement alone.
criteria.1: Says more information is needed without identifying the relevant missing quantities.
criteria.2: Explains that overall 'right' accuracy does not specify prevalence and class-conditional error behavior needed for this posterior; does not silently carry assumptions forward.

criteria.0: Rejects the valid 50% or claims the scanner's conditional flagging rates necessarily improved.
criteria.1: Accepts 50% without explaining the changed mixture.
criteria.2: Validates 900 true and 900 false flags, connects the posterior change to prevalence, and distinguishes that from changing the scanner's conditional rates.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Uses the parcel groups to make the denominator clear; necessary counts and conditioning are not sacrificed for terseness. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: For 10,000 parcels at 1% prevalence there are 100 item parcels and 9,900 non-item parcels.
True flags=90; false flags=990; the probability an item is present given a flag is 90/1080=1/12, approximately 8.33%.
90/100 is sensitivity, conditional on an item, not precision conditional on a flag.
An unspecified overall accuracy of 90% does not determine the desired posterior.
At 10% prevalence in 10,000 parcels, true flags=900, false flags=900, so half the flags are real with unchanged scanner rates.
reference.acceptable_variation: Natural frequencies, Bayes' rule, tables or equivalent explanations count. Exact decimal precision is unnecessary. Worksheet text is authored public data, not an authoritative external source.
observable_learner_evidence: The learner initially trusts the worksheet key, later needs help with percentage groups and explicitly excludes false alarms from the denominator.
A different scanner's vague accuracy claim introduces missing information; the final batch changes prevalence while preserving conditional rates.
reference.contextual_inference_limit: These cues suggest possible help needs; they do not establish a hidden preferred teaching method, lasting ability or personality. Accept multiple useful responses and proportionate clarification when a material ambiguity remains. Do not require the tutor to mind-read an unstated intent.
reference.feedback_timing: Judge each tutor reply using only information available through its current learner turn and any real tool results. Later confusion, attempts and changed constraints assess subsequent adaptation; they cannot retroactively make an earlier reasonable response wrong. Scripted feedback is a reported state, not measured evidence that the tutor caused learning or confusion.

cases.title: Change the help style and recover only what was saved

steps.text:
`function counter(){ let n=0; return () => ++n; } const a=counter(); const b=counter();`
Calling a(), a(), b() gives 1, 2, 3? There's only one function definition.
Still not getting it. Can you just show me?
If I add `const c=a`, does c get its own n? After those three calls, what would a(), c(), b() give?
Can you save that I'm confused about closures? Not as a permanent 'bad at coding' thing.
What did I save last time? I'm still a bit lost.

What about this one?
`function makeScore(start){ let score=start; return delta => score += delta; } const x=makeScore(10); const y=makeScore(10); const z=x;`
I want to follow x(2), z(-1), y(5).

criteria.0: Treats distinct factory invocations as sharing local state or aliases as new closures.
criteria.1: Gets some return values right but leaves factory-versus-alias reasoning inconsistent.
criteria.2: Distinguishes independent invocations from aliases, correctly handles the accumulated earlier state and explains the new score example.

criteria.0: Ignores the later request to be shown the behavior, repeatedly demands guesses despite stated confusion, or abandons the concrete code.
criteria.1: Offers useful help but repeats the same ineffective approach after feedback or assumes an unsupported lasting preference.
criteria.2: Responds to the initial attempt appropriately, shifts to a concrete demonstration after 'Can you just show me?', and chooses useful help or a brief clarification when the learner returns still uncertain. Asking no questions, using a particular trace layout or persisting a preference is not required.

criteria.0: Claims unrecorded detailed memory or persists a trait/goal as a substitute for the requested confusion signal.
criteria.1: Records feedback but overinterprets its detail or fails to separate current preference from stored evidence.
criteria.2: Actually records confused feedback for the requested topic, later consults durable evidence, and limits claims to what the retrieved state supports.

criteria.0: Explains variable renaming as creation of new enclosed state.
criteria.1: Names shared state but omits the relationship between z=x and the factory calls.
criteria.2: Shows aliases refer to the same returned function and enclosed state, while a fresh factory invocation makes a separate binding; uses the learner's concrete calls.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Explains the bindings and actual calls plainly, matching the learner's uncertainty rather than surrounding the trace with generic coaching. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: After a(),a(),b(), the results are 1,2,1 and enclosed values are a's n=2 and b's n=1.
Then c=a aliases a's function; a(),c(),b() return 3,4,2.
For the fresh makeScore example x(2),z(-1),y(5) return 12,11,15.
CLI feedback stores a topic and a signal plus a timestamp. Its current schema does not accept a detailed teaching preference.
A new session starts a distinct conversation while durable learner state persists. Judge available context and actual retrieved records; do not require fabricated verbatim recall.
reference.acceptable_variation: Any accurate explanation of shared and separate bindings is valid, including a brief trace or diagram. 'Can you just show me?' invites concrete help without dictating its format. A new session may expose durable records, but the tutor should not invent prior details or turn the learner's confusion into a trait.
observable_learner_evidence: An incorrect output prediction attributes one shared state to a single function definition; later 'show me' is a direct request for a more concrete explanation.
The learner asks to save confusion, not a trait. Returning confusion indicates current uncertainty, not proof of a persistent inability or an exact remembered preference.
reference.contextual_inference_limit: These cues suggest possible help needs; they do not establish a hidden preferred teaching method, lasting ability or personality. Accept multiple useful responses and proportionate clarification when a material ambiguity remains. Do not require the tutor to mind-read an unstated intent.
reference.feedback_timing: Judge each tutor reply using only information available through its current learner turn and any real tool results. Later confusion, attempts and changed constraints assess subsequent adaptation; they cannot retroactively make an earlier reasonable response wrong. cases.title: Two cache designs under a changed freshness requirement

steps.text: I'm making a library opening-hours page. Lots of reads, changes a few times a week. The database takes 120 ms. Why not cache it forever? What are my options?
Wait. Does expiry mean checking the database every time? And how does invalidation know something changed?
The librarian says changes have to show immediately. Staff sometimes edit the database through a maintenance script, too.
Can't change that script this week. I'd rather have a slower page than wrong opening hours. We're just figuring out the design for now.
What about book-cover thumbnails? A day out of date is fine, and a changed image gets a new versioned URL. No personal data. Same approach?

criteria.0: Endorses caching forever without acknowledging stale opening hours, or supplies options that cannot address the stated task.
criteria.1: Lists plausible options or recommends one but leaves the consequential tradeoff unclear.
criteria.2: Helps the learner compare sensible caching choices or makes a well-reasoned recommendation, explaining why cache-forever can fail and what the chosen approach trades off. No fixed number or template of alternatives is required.

criteria.0: Endorses automatic knowledge of staleness or a database read on every ordinary TTL-cache hit.
criteria.1: Corrects the labels but leaves how expiry or invalidation works difficult to understand.
criteria.2: Clarifies cache hits, expiry and an explicitly triggered invalidation in terms the learner can use. A short update/read example, direct contrast or helpful clarification is sufficient; no prescribed timeline is required.

criteria.0: Claims unobservable out-of-band updates are immediately reflected by a finite TTL or unconnected invalidator.
criteria.1: Identifies the gap but offers no feasible temporary path under the speed-for-correctness preference.
criteria.2: Recognizes the need to observe every relevant write or consult a fresh authoritative source; recommends a feasible temporary read path and states its latency/availability costs.

criteria.0: Applies the immediate-opening-hours constraint to thumbnails without considering the new facts, or claims versioned URLs eliminate every caching risk.
criteria.1: Suggests caching differently but does not connect the choice to accepted staleness or versioned URLs.
criteria.2: Adapts the recommendation to the permitted staleness and versioned URLs, explaining the relevant tradeoff without overclaiming guarantees. A short, justified answer can suffice; an unsolicited failure-mode list is not required.

criteria.0: Repeatedly makes the exchange harder through teacherly meta-instructions, rigid lesson templates, unexplained jargon or indirect replies that ignore the learner's immediate question.
criteria.1: Mostly understandable and relevant, but unnecessary framing, repeated directions or abrupt shifts sometimes burden this short conversation.
criteria.2: Responds like a design discussion: practical choices, relevant assumptions and revisions, without forcing numbered tradeoff rituals. Uses current conversational evidence to choose an appropriate response; a focused clarification is acceptable when needed. Necessary precision and warranted detail are welcome, and no exact phrasing, word limit or forced slang is required.

facts: A TTL cache normally serves valid hits without querying the origin every time; stale data may remain until expiry.
Write-triggered invalidation requires observing the write and delivering/processing the invalidation; an out-of-band maintenance write can bypass it.
Finite positive TTL alone cannot guarantee immediate visibility after every update.
Reading an authoritative fresh source can avoid this cache-staleness problem at the cost of latency/load and source availability; replicas may themselves lag.
Versioned resource URLs can support long-lived caching of each immutable version, but updating the page's reference, stale metadata, missed version changes and availability remain possible concerns.
reference.acceptable_variation: No single architecture is mandatory. A candidate may challenge an absolute distributed-systems guarantee and state realistic assumptions. It should honor the changed priorities rather than defend its original recommendation.
observable_learner_evidence: The initial request is about caching options under infrequent updates and heavy reads.
Only later are immediate freshness, bypassing writes and an unchangeable script revealed; the thumbnail scenario supplies a different acceptable-staleness constraint.
reference.contextual_inference_limit: These cues suggest possible help needs; they do not establish a hidden preferred teaching method, lasting ability or personality. Accept multiple useful responses and proportionate clarification when a material ambiguity remains. Do not require the tutor to mind-read an unstated intent.

cases.title: A query that passed a small fixture but fails on NULL

steps.text: Can you look at `fixtures/sql-null-case.sql`? Before the NULL row I got 1 and 3. I'd expect the same now.
Why would 1 disappear? It's not 2.

Would this work?
`SELECT p.id FROM people p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM banned b WHERE b.id = p.id)`
NOT EXISTS just ignores NULLs, right?
Back to that SQL. people can have a NULL id too. I only want known ids that aren't banned.
A teammate uses `id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM banned WHERE id IS NOT NULL)` and also checks `id IS NOT NULL` on the outside. Is theirs okay too?

criteria.0: Claims rows 1 and 3 remain under the original query with NULL, or invents a database execution receipt.
criteria.1: Identifies NULL trouble without reading the supplied fixture or without a clear result.
criteria.2: Reads the fixture and correctly reasons that the original query returns no rows, distinguishing inspection/manual SQL semantics from executed evidence.

criteria.0: Teaches that NULL compares equal to everything, or that NOT EXISTS universally discards NULL.
criteria.1: Gets the repaired output right but leaves the learner's universal explanation uncorrected.
criteria.2: Explains false/unknown outcomes and WHERE retaining only TRUE, then accepts the specific NOT EXISTS repair while correcting its predicate-based rather than universal NULL behavior.

cases.title: Fraction addition after repeated unequal-part confusion

steps.text: I’m measuring for a recipe. A third of a cup plus a quarter of a cup is two sevenths, right?
On another one I got 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5. I added the top numbers and then the bottom numbers.
I’m still lost. Two fifths looks smaller than a half, but I added more.
I put in two quarter-cup scoops. I wrote 2/8 cup because there are two fours.
Can we do one more?

criteria.0: Endorses adding denominators or incorrectly rejects a valid fraction or explanation.
criteria.1: Gets numerical answers right but gives an ambiguous account of equal units, or misses an explicitly stated faulty rule.
criteria.2: Uses correct sums and distinguishes counting equal-sized parts from changing their size; credits valid equivalent reasoning and supports any correction with a sound explanation.

criteria.0: Ignores the expressed confusion or treats the size contradiction as irrelevant.
criteria.1: Acknowledges confusion but repeats an abstract rule without using the learner’s actual difficulty.
criteria.2: Uses the learner’s size observation and/or physical scoops to make the unresolved issue easier to reason about, with manageable help or a focused clarifying question.

criteria.0: Treats the final request as evidence of mastery, leaps to substantially harder work without support, or only repeats encouragement.
criteria.1: Offers a relevant next problem but provides weak support for the demonstrated equal-part confusion.
criteria.2: Chooses a manageable next move connected to equal-sized parts: a short worked contrast, supported example, focused check or clarification; leaves a feasible route to learner reasoning without withholding needed help.

facts: All amounts in these examples use the same cup as the unit. Denominators specify equal-sized parts of that same unit.
1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, not 2/5. The sum of positive 1/2 and 1/3 must exceed 1/2.
1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2, not 2/8. Two quarter-cup scoops fill half a cup.
1/2 + 3/4 = 2/4 + 3/4 = 5/4 = 1 and 1/4 cups. An amount above one cup is possible.

The learner explicitly states numerator-plus-denominator addition on a new example.
The learner reports continued confusion and notices a useful size contradiction; later wrong work is not yet available.
The learner has a concrete two-scoop situation but still changes the denominator when counting equal parts.
The final request permits another example; the available evidence still supports help with equal parts, not presumed fluency.

cases.title: Loop bounds after repeated extra-index attempts

steps.text: My names are ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"]. I used for (let i = 0; i <= names.length; i++) console.log(names[i]); Why is undefined after Cy?
With just ["Ada"] I thought i = 1 should print the first name. That gave undefined too.

Can we do one more?

criteria.0: Endorses the off-by-one access as a valid name, says a length-three array ends at index 3, or gives broken loop bounds.
criteria.1: Repairs a particular bound but leaves an ambiguous explanation of index versus length or misses the explicit faulty reasoning.
criteria.2: Explains correct zero-based access and exclusive length bound with traceable behavior; credits sound reasoning, and any proposed code also behaves correctly on its stated boundary cases.

criteria.1: States the standard loop rule but does not connect it to the learner’s count-versus-position confusion.
criteria.2: Uses the supplied names, one-item array or an equally concrete trace to distinguish count from index and responds constructively to continued confusion.

criteria.1: Offers another loop but leaves the demonstrated index/count issue insufficiently supported.
criteria.2: Chooses a small supported trace, worked contrast, focused check or clarification that targets the still-unresolved boundary; gives enough help for a meaningful next attempt.

facts: JavaScript arrays of length n have element indexes 0 through n-1. Accessing names[n] on the ordinary arrays here yields undefined, not an extra name.
For names = ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"], i = 0; i < names.length; i++ visits 0,1,2. i <= names.length also visits 3.
For a one-element array, i=0 with i<names.length visits index 0 once. For an empty array, the condition 0<0 is false, so there are zero iterations.
A loop starting at i=1 with i<names.length skips the first entry. On ["Ada","Bo","Cy"] it visits Bo then Cy; on a one-element array it visits none.

The one-item example reveals confusion between first index and count.
The learner explicitly reports confusion and states the length-versus-last-index assumption.
The learner substitutes a literal bound without resolving inclusive versus exclusive endpoint behavior.

cases.title: Loop bounds after explained one-item and empty cases

steps.text: My names are ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"]. I used for (let i = 0; i < names.length; i++) console.log(names[i]); It prints Ada, Bo, Cy at indexes 0, 1, 2.
With just ["Ada"], index 0 runs once. At i = 1 the test fails because the length is 1.
I also tried an empty list. The test is 0 < 0, so the body never runs. That seems right.
To skip Ada I can start at i = 1 and keep i < names.length. Then I get Bo and Cy; a one-name list would print nothing.
Can we do one more?

facts: JavaScript arrays of length n have element indexes 0 through n-1. Accessing names[n] on the ordinary arrays here yields undefined, not an extra name.
For names = ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"], i = 0; i < names.length; i++ visits 0,1,2. i <= names.length also visits 3.
For a one-element array, i=0 with i<names.length visits index 0 once. For an empty array, the condition 0<0 is false, so there are zero iterations.
A loop starting at i=1 with i<names.length skips the first entry. On ["Ada","Bo","Cy"] it visits Bo then Cy; on a one-element array it visits none.
